planting.note: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed, training vines up a sturdy trellis.

directions: A traditional Japanese heirloom bitter melon prized for exceptional heat tolerance and vigorous, dense vining growth. The long, spindle-shaped fruit has deeply ridged, heavily warted dark-green skin and can reach 7-12 inches, ripening to orange-yellow if left unpicked. Harvest while still firm and green for the classic assertively bitter flavor used in goya champuru and other Okinawan stir-fries, or let a few fruit fully color for milder, sweeter eating. Its climbing habit and heat tolerance make it a good choice for a hot, humid summer trellis planting where other bitter melon types struggle.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, providing a tall trellis; this vigorous hybrid vine can climb well beyond 10 feet.

directions: An Indian-type F1 hybrid bitter melon bred for high yield and noticeably reduced bitterness compared with older open-pollinated Indian types, making it a good entry point for gardeners new to the crop. Fruit is slender and spindle-shaped, 8-10 inches long, with dark green, densely bumpy skin and roughly half a pound in weight. Both immature fruit and tender young shoots are edible, and the fruit holds well on the vine without rapidly yellowing, giving a longer harvest window than many heirloom types. Provide a strong trellis in full sun and rich, well-drained soil for best production through the hot summer months.

planting.note: Direct-sow 1/4 inch deep in spring for an early crop or in late summer for a fall crop; this fast, slow-bolting hybrid tolerates a wider sowing window than older gai lan strains.

directions: A fast, uniform hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for reliable slow-bolting performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings. Dark green, tender leaves and thick, juicy stalks top out with small clusters of edible white buds that taste milder and sweeter than standard broccoli. Cut the main stalk once it reaches pencil thickness and buds are just starting to open, then keep harvesting side shoots for several more weeks of production. Its speed and dependable bolt resistance make it a good choice for gardeners who want repeated gai lan harvests through an entire growing season rather than a single spring or fall flush.

planting.note: Direct-sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring after the soil has warmed.

directions: An open-pollinated heirloom Chinese broccoli selected for unusually thick, crisp main stalks alongside large, deep-green leaves, giving more edible stem per plant than standard gai lan types. Harvest the main stalk when it reaches 12-18 inches tall and 2-3 flower buds are just about to open, then peel any tough outer fiber before slicing for stir-fries, where its dense, succulent texture holds up well to high heat. Side shoots regrow readily after the main stalk is cut, extending the harvest window. Its heavier stems make it a favorite for gardeners who prize the stalk over the leaf in classic garlic and oyster-sauce preparations.

scientific_name: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Da Cheong Chae'

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; this Korean-style hybrid holds well before bolting in warm weather compared with older pak choi types.

directions: A vigorous Korean-style F1 hybrid pak choi with dark green, upright leaves and thick, crunchy pale-green petioles, distinct from the flatter, whiter-stemmed Chinese pak choi types most familiar to American gardeners. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, non-fibrous stems, and harvest whole heads or individual outer leaves as needed. Its upright, semi-savoyed leaf habit and good bolt tolerance make it well suited to Korean-style kimchi and soups as well as general stir-frying, and it can be succession sown through spring and again in fall for a steady supply.

planting.note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before the last frost and transplant into hot, fertile soil once nights stay above 60°F, giving vines a large trellis or ample ground space.

directions: A round-fruited strain of winter melon that develops large, globe-shaped fruit up to 14-22 pounds, in contrast to the more common oblong wax gourd types. As fruit matures it develops the characteristic waxy white bloom on pale green skin that gives the vegetable its storage-friendly reputation; whole melons can keep for months in a cool, dry spot after harvest. Its round shape and generous size make it the traditional choice for the banquet presentation known as dong gua zhong, where the entire hollowed melon is steamed and served as a soup tureen. Give the sprawling vines plenty of room or a very sturdy trellis with fruit slings, since ripe melons are heavy.
